title: The GitHub Actions Ecosystem
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of the github actions ecosystem and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to the github actions ecosystem.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content_blocks.code:
name: Inspect workflow metadata
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  inspect:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Print non-sensitive context
        env:
          REPOSITORY: ${{ github.repository }}
          REF_NAME: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: echo "Repository=$REPOSITORY ref=$REF_NAME"
content_blocks.expected_output: The log shows the repository and ref name for the manually started run without printing secrets.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run it on a test branch and verify the values match the selected repository and ref.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Delete the sample workflow when the context example is no longer needed.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to the github actions ecosystem. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain the github actions ecosystem, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Understand why automation belongs beside source control and how events become repeatable work.

content.task: Apply the github actions ecosystem to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: The main workflow objects are events, jobs, steps, actions, expressions, permissions, and runners; together they define when work starts and how results are produced.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: The main workflow objects are events, jobs, steps, actions, expressions, permissions, and runners; together they define when work starts and how results are produced. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: The main workflow objects are events, jobs, steps, actions, expressions, permissions, and runners; together they define when work starts and how results are produced.
Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
